cells.tense: You are here with the pen, and the room is meeting you back.
cells.ask: Pick one group — three people, a household, a standing call. Take one even step into their middle, and take it at the same size again next week.
cells.core:
You read a room before you act, and you read it fairly. When someone feels crowded and someone else feels turned away from, you move without being asked until the two of them have a little air and a little ground. That happens before anyone says the word, and it's why the ones close to you can say the harder thing to you than they can to most.

What this is for is that the fairness holds and the room stays able to feel. So pick one group — three people, a household, a standing call — and take one even step into their middle, the same size again next week, until the balance holds when you step back. You'll know it landed by how the week runs.
cells.sheetLine: You keep the room fair by hand, and you're allowed to stop carrying it alone.
cells.verb: keeping the room fair, one feeling at a time
cells.place: the scale a person re-weights by hand

cells.tense: For the week that hasn't started yet, you'll have read everyone before anyone has to say a word.
cells.act: release what is done and keep what serves
cells.ask: Before the meal or the meeting, take two names off the list. Two people you won't watch for, two comments you won't soften. Then let the hour arrive as it is.
cells.core:
You're kept in step with the mood wherever people gather, and that's what's getting spent. You have the small correction ready before the first voice turns sharp. You make a sentence gentler early so nobody has to feel its edge. That's not a fault. At this pitch it has to run on guesses — about how a person will take it, about the thing they might say — and a guess, spent carefully, costs the day.

Most of what you're bracing for doesn't arrive, so before the meal or the meeting, take two names off the list. Two people you won't watch for tonight, two comments you won't make easier for anyone. Keep whatever you actually sense once people are assembled. The rest is charged to tomorrow, and tomorrow already carries enough.

cells.tense: For the last while you have stood beside the fairness, and today the door feels closed from your side.
cells.act: tell the truth with care for when and how
cells.ask: Pick a room you were in this week and write one flat sentence of what happened. Don't polish it, don't explain it, and don't send it anywhere.
cells.core:
You can describe what happened in any room with complete accuracy, and none of it moves you. The fairness is still under your feet somewhere. You remember its weight in your hands. Today the way things read has folded into a few flat sentences: this happened, that happened, that's how it is. Naming a room from the outside is not the same as standing in it.

So pick a room you were in this week and write one flat sentence of what happened. Leave it unpolished. Don't explain it, and don't send it to anyone. On a slow day, writing the true thing without decoration is enough to put weight back into a stance you thought you'd lost.
cells.sheetLine: You can describe the fairness perfectly. You stopped standing on it.
cells.verb: keeping the room fair, one feeling at a time
cells.place: the scale a person re-weights by hand

cells.tense: Right now you keep the room's fairness moving, and the account you give of it is maintenance.
cells.act: cut to the logic and act on it
cells.ask: Name the one gathering you're holding level. Whoever asks about the two people and their space, answer plainly that you've been keeping it steady.
cells.core:
You are the one balancing things. You've done it for a stretch in which two people keep missing each other, and it has stayed level because you step in early, before the air gets thin. When asked, you say the two of them just needed space, and the space looks like nobody's doing anything. What's standing is standing because you keep re-weighting it, and 'space' is the name the account gives the work your hands do.

Name the one gathering you're holding level. Next time someone asks how things got better between those two, answer plainly that you've been keeping it steady. No strategy, no system. The next time the ledger shifts, you'll know whose hand moved it.
